q: Am I peeing? What is that fluid?

blocks.x: Oh god, am I peeing? This is wrong. What if he thinks it's gross?
It isn't urine, and this isn't folklore, it's been confirmed in a lab.
Female ejaculation is a much smaller amount, whitish, thicker, from a real gland. Squirting is a larger gush, usually urine.
The shame drops out almost immediately, once there's a real, named, studied structure standing where the confusion used to be.

q: Is my body finished after menopause?

blocks.x: I'm in menopause. For a while, everything down there felt dry, closed, done.
The first time my body actually let go, I wasn't expecting it. A shimmer. A trickle. A slow, quiet letting go, at an age I'd been quietly told this was finished.
The most precise map of this anatomy that science has ever produced came from two postmenopausal women.
If you've quietly filed some part of your body under over and done, the science doesn't support that filing system. Neither does mine.

q: Where do I start when I can't stand being touched right now?

blocks.x: Pushing through does not work. Every time you let it happen and go somewhere else while it does, you teach your body that its signal changed nothing.

The Breath Bridge. It asks nothing at all of your skin, which is exactly why it goes first. Sit facing each other, close enough to feel the warmth coming off him, not touching. Breathe four in, hold for two, six out. Three minutes on a timer. When the timer goes, one word each. Then you stop.
The Three Breath Hold. Reach for his hand. Do not speak. Three slow breaths together. Nothing that leads anywhere. A hand is allowed to be only a hand.
It gets louder before it gets quieter. Nothing has gone wrong when that happens.

q: What is he seeing when I pull away?

blocks.x: He is walking into completely different weather every day with no forecast.
He cannot see the skin change. He cannot see the pain forecast. He gets one piece of information, which is that his arms are not wanted, and he draws the only conclusion available to him.
So he stops reaching. Then you have the distance as well as everything else.

q: Sex has been hurting. Why does even a hug feel like a warning?

blocks.x: If sex has been hurting, your body has been running a pain forecast for a while now.
Pain produces watchfulness. Watchfulness produces tension, including in the pelvic floor. That tension increases the pain. Round and round.
That much is documented for genital pain. Whether it reaches all the way out to a pair of arms at the kettle, nobody has studied. I watch it reach.
His arms arrive meaning I love you. Your nervous system receives here we go again. Both of those are true accounts of the same fifteen seconds.

q: Why do I pull away when he hugs me?

blocks.x: Oestrogen runs your skin too. As it drops, the barrier gets leakier and holds less water.
So the surface his hand lands on is a different surface from the one he was landing on five years ago.
Women describe the change as though it happened to their feelings. They tell me they have gone cold, that they are worried they do not love him anymore.

When we slow down and get specific about what happens in the two seconds after contact, it is almost always happening at the level of skin, and nervous system, and what the body has learned to expect.
Being touched isn't the same as feeling touch. Patterns can be changed.

q: Am I with the wrong person, or do I just have low libido?

blocks.x: The woman who is genuinely with the wrong person usually knows it, in a way that is hard to unknow.
You were never taught to know what you want, or to ask for it out loud.
Somewhere in there, your own wanting got so quiet that you genuinely cannot tell anymore whether it is gone, or whether it was simply never asked to speak.
Say out loud, to him, exactly how you take your tea, the real and specific version.
Then do one more round, with touch: ask him to touch your arm exactly the way you want it, and adjust him until it is right.
You are teaching your body that your wanting is allowed to take up space.

q: What does it mean when she says she is fine but her whole body changes?

blocks.x: When she says she is fine and her body tells a different story, she has learned to override.
The body says one thing and the social self says another, and she has been practising this since long before she met you.
These are signals to read.
The man who can read them, imperfectly, just enough to notice, is the man she relaxes into.
Her nervous system has registered: he sees me.

q: What is happening in her body when she goes quiet?

blocks.x: When she goes quiet at the dinner table, something specific is happening in her body.
Her system has detected something it needs to process.
It has pulled resources inward.
The silence is the body working.

q: How do I figure out what I actually like in bed?

blocks.x: You do not think your way to the answer.
Choose one place on your own skin.
Touch it one way: slow, barely-there, almost not touching at all.
Touch the exact same place a second way: firmer, with more contact, more decision in the hand.
One of those will have landed more than the other.
That is your body, answering a question out loud for the first time in years.

q: Why do I go blank when he asks me what I like?

blocks.x: Losing contact with your own needs so completely that you genuinely do not know what you want.
It happens to a body that spent years reading the room for everyone else's cues, until the wiring for its own went quiet.
Under the blank tape is a body that still knows exactly what it wants.
It just stopped being asked.
None of that is a character flaw.
It is a body doing exactly what it was trained to do.

q: Why do I worry about his orgasm more than my own pleasure?

blocks.x: A great many of us cannot receive.
What we cannot do is lie back and let ourselves be the point without immediately trying to pay it off.
We were taught that our job is to make sure he is alright.
The next time a man gives you pleasure, do the radical thing.
Receive it.
Do not keep score.

q: How do I tell him what I want without ruining the mood?

blocks.x: The next time your body wants something other than what is happening, say it.
One sentence.
"Slower." "Here." "Like that."
Watch what he does.
They are starving to know.

q: Why can she feel it with someone else but not with me?

blocks.x: The pleasure could move because the pleasure was free.
Your hand carries the whole weight of the marriage.
The more a touch matters, the harder the body braces.
The man she loves most gets the most guarded body, precisely because he is the one she cannot afford to be wrong with.
It was waiting for the touch to cost less.
None of this is your fault.

q: She lights up around other men. What should I do, and what should I not do?

blocks.x: Confronting her about the instructor.
You will make her ashamed of the one bit of aliveness she has access to, and a body cannot open from shame.
You cannot out-perform your way out of a stakes pattern.
The candlelit weekend designed to fix it carries its own enormous price tag.
Touch her with nowhere for it to go.
When she braces, stay.

q: Why does she tighten up when I reach for her, and why do I pull back?

blocks.x: She reads the pulling back as abandonment.
He reads her tightening as rejection, or a test, or something he has already failed.
When she tightens, you are watching a nervous system do what nervous systems were built to do.
Her body has moved before her mind caught up.
Her closing is a response to something neither of you has had the language for yet.
Patterns can be changed.

q: What do I do when she closes and every instinct says to leave?

blocks.x: The difference is that with her, your own system gets activated first.
This is not easy.
Every instinct says walk away, fix it, wait for it to pass.
The moment you stay when everything in you wants to leave.
That is the moment that changes things.
Your presence is the safest thing you have.

q: Why does my body still reach for him at 3am when I'm the one who left?

blocks.x: Bodies do not read divorce papers.
They keep reaching for what they were shaped around, long after the mind has signed off.
The leaving was a decision.
The unwiring was a process.
They run on completely different clocks.
The decision can be right and the body can still grieve.

q: How do I get through the 3am reach without texting him?

blocks.x: When you uncouple, you do not stop having a body.
If you do not give it somewhere honest to go, it will reach backwards.
The work here is to give the grief a structured place to move, and to teach the body it can be soothed and steadied without going back to the thing it is leaving.
Through Touch you choose.
Through your own hands.
Through a practice you can do alone at 3am instead of texting him.

q: Can an old scar make me numb or take away sensation during sex?

blocks.x: A caesarean scar can shut down pelvic sensation.
An episiotomy scar can blunt arousal.
The internal adhesions can persist for decades.
Women carrying caesarean scars commonly report numbness across the lower belly, reduced sensation across the vulva, pain during deep penetration, a sense that the lower body has gone quiet.
The medical record says: healed without complication.
The body says something else.

q: Why does my body refuse to relax in my partner's arms? Is something wrong with me?

blocks.x: Years later, the woman tries to relax in her partner's arms and her body refuses, and she does not know why, and she begins to believe there is something wrong with her.
There is nothing wrong with her.
Her body is doing exactly what it learned to do to keep her alive.

q: Why did my body open up so fast to someone who turned out not to be safe?

blocks.x: The nervous system that has been touch-starved will reach for the first thing that feels like nourishment.
This is survival.
It felt held and opened toward more holding.
That is biology.
Your body did not fail you.
It did exactly what it was designed to do in the presence of what looked like safety.

q: Why am I the only one who notices what needs doing?

blocks.x: The noticing is what exhausts you.
That question, well meant as it is, hands the thinking straight back to her, because now she has to notice the gap, translate it into a task, and hand it to him in a form he can execute.
What actually redistributes it is fifteen minutes, one prompt, and a structure that makes it safe for both of you to actually hear the answer.
Set a timer.
"TELL ME WHAT I CAN DO TO LIGHTEN THE LOAD. WHAT DO YOU NEED ME TO DO?"
Do this once a week.

q: Why does my partner flinch when I touch her?

blocks.x: Her body is running a pattern it built long before you, to protect itself from touch that might turn into a demand it cannot meet.
Rejection has nothing to do with it.
Somewhere she learned that once touch starts, she has to see it through.
So her body started guarding the door.
That is a pattern in her nervous system, and it says nothing about your desirability.
You have more power over it than anyone has told you.

q: What can I do so she stops flinching?

blocks.x: Touch her once, deliberately, with no outcome attached.
A hand on her shoulder as you pass.
A palm flat on her back for three seconds.
Then take your hand away first, and carry on with what you were doing.
No lingering to see if it becomes more.
Do that for a week, and her body starts to learn that your hand is not a bill coming due.

q: Why is my haircut the only time anyone touches me?

blocks.x: Skin hunger.
A body reporting an actual deficit.
It carries a set of nerve fibres, C-tactile afferents, that fire specifically for slow, warm, gentle contact at roughly the speed of a stroke down a forearm.
When that traffic goes quiet for long enough, the body doesn't simply carry on unbothered.
Sleep gets worse.
The baseline hum of alertness climbs.

q: How do I give myself the Touch I'm missing?

blocks.x: It knows slow, it knows warm, it knows predicted.
Your own hands qualify.
One hand flat on your chest, one hand on your belly.
One minute, no more.
You are noticing two things: the warmth of your own hands coming back at you through your own skin, and the breath moving underneath them.
A body that cannot receive its own Touch will struggle to receive anyone else's.

q: Why did I cry when I gave my body a minute of real contact?

blocks.x: The first is that the hunger gets louder before it gets quieter.
A body that's been running on almost nothing tends to go quiet about it, and then you give it a minute of real contact and it remembers, all at once, what it's been going without.
Some people cry the first week doing something this small.
If that's you, nothing has gone wrong.
That's a channel opening after a long time closed.

q: Why did the spark die after the first few months?

blocks.x: What they mean is the intensity dropped.
The body experiences it as the absence of a signal it was trained to interpret as love.
What the body was reading as love was recognition.
When the storm calms and oxytocin begins to replace dopamine as the primary bonding hormone, the body enters a different register.
Warmth instead of fire.
If you recognise what I am describing, you are not failing at your relationship.

q: Why does a calm, kind partner feel flat to me?

blocks.x: The body scans for the old signal, cannot find it, and produces a feeling of flatness that gets interpreted as "the spark has gone."
For many of my clients, the hardest thing is tolerating safety.
Being in a room with someone who is not going to leave, not going to explode, not going to withdraw.
The body scans for danger and finds none.
Instead of relaxing, it panics.
What it transforms into looks like a hand on your back that you lean into without thinking.

q: How do I help her feel safe with me when I don't know what to do?

blocks.x: Stay close to her. Close enough that she can feel your body near hers.
Your body stays soft. Jaw unclenched. Hands open. Breath slow.
Say: tell me what is happening for you right now.
Then stop. The silence is where she finds her own words.
When she speaks, you say: thank you. Clarify that. Summarise that.
Now take that attention out of your head and put it in your body. Stay close. Stay.

q: Why can I explain exactly why he is the way he is, but I can't say what I want?

blocks.x: That's the swap.
Hers goes unexamined, sometimes for a relationship's worth of years.
A woman arrives fluent in her partner's nervous system and can't tell me the last time she checked in with her own.
It's just where the attention has been trained to go, on him, always on him, because examining him feels like doing something, and examining herself feels like admitting something.
The thing that's been quietly changing is what you want now, at this age, in this body, and you haven't asked yourself that question in years.
Notice one place on your own body you'd actually like touched, before anyone touches you. Don't say it out loud yet.
Just notice it.

q: How do I tell her I need touch without it sounding like I want sex?

blocks.x: She's learned, across hundreds of small moments, that physical touch from you comes with a destination attached, and that if she receives it and then does not travel to that destination, there will be an atmosphere she has to manage later.
Reach for her with nowhere to go, and then actually go nowhere. Once, maybe twice today. Not more.
Small repeated doses beat one brave conversation, every time. A body rebuilds trust the way it builds muscle, in reps.
After two weeks, when there's some evidence on the table, you can say it.
I want to tell you something about me, and I'm not asking you for anything tonight. Touch is how I feel connected to you.
Then stop talking.

q: Why does she tense up or pull away when I touch her, even when I mean it kindly?

blocks.x: In her body and psyche, for a long time, a hand has never only been a hand.
So her body stopped receiving. Receiving simply became expensive, no cruelty in it meant at all.
You are asking her mind to override a track record her body keeps. Better wording will not do it.
Before you reach, ask, out loud, plainly: “Where are you right now, on a scale of braced to open?”
If the answer is braced, you don't reach, you just know
If the answer is open, that's when the hand you've been building evidence for gets to land.

q: She was so open with me, and now she's cold and distant. Did I do something wrong?

blocks.x: A nervous system can only hold so much openness at once.
Open past the edge of it, even into something good, especially into something good, and the body does what it's always done when it's taken in more than it can metabolise.
It closes to catch up.
She is often as surprised by the cold as you are.
She didn't vanish, and you weren't wrong.
She went to the place her body goes to recover from having trusted you.

q: She has pulled away after we got close. What do I do now?

blocks.x: Stay close enough that she can feel you haven't gone anywhere, far enough that she isn't being pressed.
Let the retreat be allowed. Don't make her pay for being cold with your face.
Give her one signal that costs her nothing to receive, and then leave her be.
Bring her a cup of tea, put it down beside her with no question attached, no pulling for approval.
Reach with nowhere to go, and then actually go nowhere. Do not linger to see what happened.

A man who can meet that without collapsing and without attacking teaches her body something it may never have been taught. That she can open, and close, and open again, and the door will still be there.

q: Why do I go cold or tearful after we've been really close?

blocks.x: I would open, occasionally, all the way, have the most beautiful connective time, and then I'd go quiet for days.
I would be tearful after sex and call it hormones, being tired, or “just the way I am”.
I just didn't have the language then that I have now.
Sensation as language.
The understanding that the body is reporting when it retreats.
There was a moment when you approached me and my back tightened, my jaw stiffened, and my heart rate sped up.

q: Someone I love is hurting badly and I don't know what to say. How do I stay with them?

blocks.x: Set the container first. Say: I have time. I am not going to fix anything. I just want to know what it is like for you right now.
Tell me what is happening in your body right now.
Tell me what you need right now that nobody is giving you.
After each answer, only three responses. No fixing. No jumping to the next question.
Thank you, I heard you. Clarify that, say more. Summarise that, give me the one thing at the centre.
Then stay in the silence for a moment before you move on.

q: How can I tell when she is starting to tense up, before she says anything?

blocks.x: By the time you notice she has gone tense, her body has already been bracing for between two and seven seconds.
Before the visible brace, there is a held inhale that does not finish.
Watch the rhythm of her chest. The unbraced breath has a soft drop at the end of every exhale.
You can drop your own breath. Audibly. A long, quiet exhale that softens your shoulders. You do not say anything. You do not ask what is wrong.
If your body says we are safe, we have time, nothing has to happen here, hers will start to remember that.

q: She says she's fine, but I can tell she isn't. How do I know what she really means?

blocks.x: The smile did not reach her eyes. The yes was a fraction of a second too fast.
Her body voted no while her mouth voted yes.
She is performing a survival skill she learned when lying was the safer option.
That looks like: not getting hurt or defensive when something difficult is named. Not making her responsible for your reaction.
If you can sit, in your own body, with whatever she is bringing, without flinching, without fixing, without making it about you, her override will start to loosen. Over weeks.
The body learns slowly because the body has been collecting evidence for a long time. You are giving it new evidence.

q: She used to open up to me and now she doesn't. What am I missing?

blocks.x: Her body, even when it has been bracing for years, opens. Briefly. In windows. Often without her knowing.
The opening looks specific. The breath drops into the belly. The shoulders fall and stay fallen. The eye contact lengthens by a beat.
The window is small. Often three to seven seconds. If nothing is done with it, it closes. Her body learns that its openings do not lead anywhere.
When you catch one, you do not have to do anything dramatic. You stop. You meet her eyes. You let your own body soften in response. You do not name it. Naming it usually closes it. You receive it.
Over months, her system rebuilds its trust in opening because the openings have started to land somewhere.

q: Why is my body always tense, and where does it come from?

blocks.x: The response does not evaporate when the event ends.
The body files it.
It goes into the tissue as tension, as bracing. As a set of the jaw. A grip in the low back. A pair of shoulders that have not fully dropped since you were nine.
Bound energy. Held as protection. Often for decades.
You stop noticing it the way you stop hearing a fridge hum. It becomes the temperature of being you.
A body that is never allowed to put its bracing down will eventually find its own way to lay you flat.

q: Why did I shake, cry or laugh when my body let go?

blocks.x: That letting go rarely looks tidy.
Bodies on my table shake. They tremble. They stretch into shapes no one taught them.

q: Something hard was just said and the air has gone heavy. What do I do?

blocks.x: You stop trying to fix what just happened. You name that something has changed. Something just shifted between us. Or the air just changed. Or something landed for you. You do not interpret it. You do not assign blame.

You do nothing for a moment. You do not move toward her physically unless your body is calm. You do not move away. You let your own body settle. You drop your shoulders. You take one slow breath that ends in a soft exhale.
Once you have named the air and let your body settle, you can ask one question. Not interrogating. Not fixing. Do you want to tell me what landed for you? Or simpler: I am here when you are ready.
The phrasing matters less than the absence of pressure.
The window may be three minutes. It may be three days.

q: Why does she go blank and can't talk after something hard is said?

blocks.x: Most importantly, she is not deciding to be like this.
Her body has done it for her. The decision happened in milliseconds, before language arrived. She is now living inside a state her body produced as protection.
Trying to reach her with words at this point is like trying to call across a canyon. She can hear sound. She cannot quite reach the meaning.
Her access to language and connection has briefly gone offline. Asking for one is asking for something her system cannot produce.
The body has to come back first.

q: Why do I freeze, go cold or get angry when she is upset?

blocks.x: Your body responded the way it learned to respond a long time ago. Maybe at three. Maybe at seven.
Some men go into fixing mode. The mind starts running options. The body leans forward.
Some men go cold. The body pulls back.
Some men go hot. Anger arrives almost instantly, often surprising them with how fast.
I have worked with enough men to know that the heat under the anger is grief.
None of this is your fault. You were never taught what to do here.

q: Why do I feel disgusted when he touches me?

blocks.x: Disgust was built as a rejection response, the body's way of saying this does not come in.
Disgust is the last move your body makes. It has already tried everything quieter.
When that gets missed too, month after month, year after year, the body stops spending energy on signals that never worked. It goes straight to the biggest lever it has left.
Your body is using the only language that has ever produced a result.
Your body is responding to the next forty minutes it has learned to expect from that hand.
When touch has meant one thing for long enough, the body stops processing contact and starts processing the sequence.

q: If I just wait, will the feeling go away? What actually helps?

blocks.x: You have been sold the idea that desire is spontaneous, that it will simply return if you are patient and the conditions are right. It does not come back on its own, because nothing has changed about what your body is predicting.
You let it happen and you go somewhere else while it does. Every time you do that you teach your body that its biggest signal changes nothing, and next time it must come in louder or earlier.
You take the destination off the table, out loud, for a fixed period.
Six weeks, and both of you know it in advance. Nothing is allowed to lead anywhere.
Once the body stops predicting the arc, a hand goes back to being a hand.

q: Why can I handle quick, functional touch but slow, tender touch feels unbearable?

blocks.x: I call it the Armour. It contains in order to stay safe, and its particular signature is that softness feels dangerous where pressure does not.
Women in the Armour can often manage brisk, functional, sexual touch far better than they can manage tenderness. A hand held gently for too long is unbearable in a way that nothing rough ever is.
It gets louder before it gets quieter. A body that has been overridden for years will, given a genuine opening, tell you the size of the backlog all at once.
Nothing has gone wrong when that happens. That is a channel opening after a long time shut.

q: Why do I feel nothing when my partner touches me? What is wrong with me?

blocks.x: Your body has a window, a range it can stay present and feel inside. Stress, exhaustion, years of bracing all shrink that window until there is barely any room left in it.

When touch arrives at the edge of a window narrowed to a slit, your body does the only intelligent thing left. It checks out. It goes numb because feeling has become more than it can hold right now, even though nothing in you is truly gone.
You brace a half-second before he touches you. You leave your body during sex and plan tomorrow's list. You perform relaxed at dinner while something in you stands guard.
That is a nervous system with no spare capacity, protecting you the only way it knows.
Desire cannot move into a body that has no room. First you make room.

q: What can I do to start feeling touch again?

blocks.x: Ask him for three minutes of touch that is not allowed to lead anywhere. A hand on your arm. Your back stroked.
Notice what your body is literally doing.
The plain physical facts. Warmth here. Tightness there. A flutter. A held breath. A wanting to pull away.
If your body wants to flinch, let it, and notice that.
Three minutes, then stop on purpose, while it still feels safe. Tomorrow, three minutes again.
You are widening the window desire can walk back through.

q: Why was it so intense at the beginning, and now it feels flat? Has the passion died?

blocks.x: The ones who come to me at month nine, year two, year five, saying the passion died. What they mean is the intensity dropped.

The early months of a relationship are often a neurochemical storm: dopamine flooding the reward centres, norepinephrine creating the racing heart and inability to eat, cortisol suppressing the rational brain.
It is the body's way of bonding before the slower, deeper chemistry of attachment takes over.

When the storm calms and oxytocin begins to replace dopamine as the primary bonding hormone, the body enters a different register. Warmth instead of fire. Safety instead of urgency. Ease instead of ache.
You are not failing at your relationship.
The passion transforms. What it transforms into looks like a hand on your back that you lean into without thinking. A silence in the kitchen that does not need filling.

q: My wife has gone quiet and says it's not me. What does she need from me?

blocks.x: What her body needs is a man who does not flinch. Who can stand in the same room as something this heavy without needing her to shrink it so you stay comfortable.
When there is an opening, she needs the one thing almost every man reaches for last. Touch that asks for nothing.
Sex is a question her nervous system cannot answer right now.

A hand laid flat between her shoulder blades and left there long enough that it stops being a question. Your palm on the back of her neck while the kettle boils. Sitting close enough that your arm rests against hers through a whole film and you do not move it toward anything.
Intimacy was never spontaneous. It is built, from the least dramatic touch in the house.
Do not ask what you did. Put your hand flat between her shoulder blades. Leave it there. Want nothing from it.

q: Why does my body tense up or go still the moment my partner reaches for me?

blocks.x: Speed and height read as intention to a nervous system before a single thought forms about it.
Hands that arrive high and fast are read as reaching for something. Hands that arrive low and slow are read as staying.
A body that's bracing for someone reaching cannot, at the same time, open for someone staying.
High and fast, she holds. Low and slow, she opens.

q: When my partner reaches for me and I feel myself stiffen, what can I actually do?

blocks.x: So next time your partner reaches for you and you feel yourself stiffen:
Move his hands, slowly, exactly to where you want them. That is the bravest action.
Watch what happens when you do. The breath drops. The shoulders come down.
Warm. Weight. Where.
That word is your body telling you the truth, and you get to follow it, be that specific.

q: She flinches when I reach for her. What should I do?

blocks.x: You have been taught that wanting her means reaching for her. So you reach, and she goes somewhere you cannot follow, and you start to think it is you.
She is guarding a nervous system that never gets to stand down, not once, not even in her sleep.
So the move is the moment she flinches, because she will. Do not pull your hand back, and do not push it on.
Leave it soft and still, and say, no rush, I am not going anywhere.
You have just handed her body the one thing it never gets. Permission to take its time.
Let her arrive before you move. She sets the pace. You keep it.

q: Why won't my body relax and open up, even when I want it to?

blocks.x: The autonomic nervous system scans continuously for signs of danger or safety.
What it reads as safe is predictability: when the brain can anticipate what comes next, the vigilance load reduces.
A nervous system organised around threat does not open on demand.
The body learning, session by session, that it is allowed to stay open for longer each time.

q: Why do I freeze or go blank when I try to touch my own body slowly?

blocks.x: Sometimes the system simply stops.
Be curious about your body. Do this exact exercise again in a few days and see what is different.
The willingness to return to the body without already knowing the answer.

q: Why am I so afraid of him leaving when he has given me no reason?

blocks.x: when a client tells me their fear is irrational, that nothing in their life explains it, they are sometimes right. The fear has a source. The source does not belong to them.
trauma does not disappear when the person who experienced it dies.
If the caregiver's body is organised around the threat of disappearance, the child's nervous system inherits that organisation as though it were the correct response to reality.
when you understand that the fear is inherited, you do not have to defend against it anymore.
You do not have to explain it to your partner.

q: Why do I go numb or flinch when I'm touched, even by someone I love?

blocks.x: The mind seals the room to let you grow up and function. The body keeps everything.
The bracing. The half-second flinch before contact. The desire that thins out for no reason you can name.

q: What does it mean when she says "I'm fine" but clearly isn't?

blocks.x: "Fine" is the last word her body could get past the door before the true one was ready.
